selected.lesson_subject: Multicast policy NAT and VDOM loop prevention: interface scope, source/destination translation, and all-to-all hazards
selected.scenario_status: No directly matched Community scenario published within 2026-10-25 through 2026-11-24 was verified.
selected.feature_mechanism_fingerprint: NAT-mode multicast forwarding is a separate packet-forwarding gate; multicast-policy objects match ingress/egress interfaces, source address, multicast group, protocol and port, and can apply multicast SNAT/DNAT; all-to-all policies can create a loop across same-VDOM NPU virtual links in multi-VDOM mode.
selected.workflow_transaction_fingerprint: Multicast packet enters interface -> multicast-forward gate permits forwarding domain -> multicast-policy match evaluates source/destination interface and address/group -> optional source/destination translation -> packet exits selected interface; TTL and multicast-router function remain distinct from policy NAT.
selected.failure_class: Unintended multicast flood or loop; policy match miss; translated source/group not as expected.
selected.evidence_pattern: show system settings multicast-forward; show firewall multicast-policy; policy hit/log evidence; packet capture before/after translation; VDOM/interface inventory for npu0_vlink0/npu0_vlink1.
selected.remediation_path: Replace any-to-any policy with explicit interface and multicast-group scope; define source/group objects; use SNAT/DNAT only where receiver/source design requires it; remove same-VDOM all-to-all loop path before enabling multi-VDOM; do not enable multicast forwarding if FortiGate is acting as multicast router.
selected.question_fingerprint: Differentiate forwarding gate from multicast routing; identify the policy object that performs SNAT; detect NPU virtual-link multicast loop; infer what a TTL decrement proves.
selected.diagram_topology_layout_fingerprint: Multicast source -> FortiGate forwarding gate -> policy match -> optional NAT -> receiver segment, with separate loop-back path between same-VDOM NPU virtual links.

selected.lesson_subject: FortiManager HA state replication and failover: heartbeat, synchronized databases, excluded local settings, and VRRP
selected.scenario_status: Recent Community scenario published 2026-11-13; used only to illustrate why FDS health should be checked independently on both HA peers, not as the primary HA feature source.
selected.feature_mechanism_fingerprint: FortiManager primary stores database changes and synchronizes module data/configuration to one or more secondary peers; TCP/5199 heartbeat and sync links maintain cluster state; VRRP mode uses shared VIP and monitored interface, while manual mode requires explicit role promotion; multiple system-local settings and downloaded FortiGuard data are excluded from sync.
selected.workflow_transaction_fingerprint: Admin change on primary -> database commit -> module/configuration synchronization to peers -> heartbeat exchange -> monitored-interface failure detection -> VRRP secondary becomes primary and owns VIP/FGFM path, or operator promotes peer in manual mode.
selected.failure_class: Split expectations after failover: unsynchronized local settings, heartbeat loss, VIP/interface failure, or managed devices still targeting old primary.
selected.evidence_pattern: System Settings > HA cluster status; Module Data Synchronized/Pending Module Data; HA debug log; TCP/5199 reachability; per-peer FortiGuard update status; managed-device FGFM registration.
selected.remediation_path: Use identical model/firmware and cluster ID/group password; define peer IP/SN on both sides; isolate HA/sync interface; choose manual or VRRP intentionally; configure managed FortiGates with all peer addresses; separately replicate excluded local services/settings and validate both peers.
selected.question_fingerprint: Identify which FortiManager data is not synchronized; distinguish heartbeat from module replication; select correct failover mode; explain why FDS success on primary does not prove peer readiness.
selected.diagram_topology_layout_fingerprint: Administrator -> primary FortiManager -> secondary peers over TCP/5199 sync/heartbeat; separate managed FortiGate FGFM path and VRRP shared VIP with monitored interface.

selected.lesson_subject: Privacy masking in administrator profiles: field anonymization, key-based unmasking, and time-window boundaries
selected.scenario_status: No directly matched Community scenario published within the strict 30-day window was verified.
selected.feature_mechanism_fingerprint: Privacy masking is attached to an administrator profile, masks selected identity/host/message fields across modules and reports, produces per-administrator anonymization that changes at login, and permits selective key-authorized unmasking subject to a 0-365-day time window.
selected.workflow_transaction_fingerprint: Admin profile selects fields + data mask key + unmasked time -> profile assigned to admin -> queries/reports render masked values -> user invokes Screen Picker or Manual Input -> key validates and selected field is revealed within time policy.
selected.failure_class: Sensitive data exposed to overprivileged operator, expected field appears unmasked, unmask denied, or downloaded log lacks original values.
selected.evidence_pattern: Admin profile settings; same event viewed under masked and unmasked profiles; See Original Data dialog; log download; real-time versus historical/custom-view/drill-down comparison.
selected.remediation_path: Create least-privilege profile, mask required fields, securely distribute data-mask key, set shortest viable unmask window, test real-time and historical views separately, and use a separate controlled export path when original values are required.
selected.question_fingerprint: Explain per-login anonymization; identify why downloaded logs omit masked values; distinguish real-time log behavior from time-window masking; choose safe unmask workflow.
selected.diagram_topology_layout_fingerprint: Log source -> FortiAnalyzer view/report -> administrator-profile masking layer -> anonymized output, with a separate key-authorized unmask path.

selected.lesson_subject: FortiSwitch IP conflict detection: passive ARP ownership claims and active gratuitous-ARP probes
selected.scenario_status: No directly matched recent Community scenario was verified; older switch onboarding/PoE articles were rejected as unrelated.
selected.feature_mechanism_fingerprint: Global FortiSwitch management-interface conflict detection combines passive observation of remote broadcast ARP source addresses with active gratuitous-ARP probes at boot, interface down-to-up and local IP change; a duplicate response generates a system log and SNMP trap.
selected.workflow_transaction_fingerprint: Remote ARP claim arrives -> compare sender IP with local system-interface IPs -> log/trap; separately, local event triggers GARP broadcast -> duplicate owner replies -> log conflict.
selected.failure_class: Duplicate management IP, wrong ARP ownership, or monitoring gap when trap delivery is not configured.
selected.evidence_pattern: System log 'IP Conflict: conflict detected on system interface ...'; SNMP ip-conflict trap; `show system global` and `set detect-ip-conflict`; packet capture of ARP/GARP.
selected.remediation_path: Identify both MAC/IP owners from ARP capture and switch CAM table; correct static/DHCP reservation or interface address; keep global detection enabled; configure SNMP trap recipients and verify both log and trap.
selected.question_fingerprint: Differentiate passive claim detection from active GARP; determine what a GARP reply proves; interpret trap versus log; avoid claiming this scans every endpoint in the subnet.
selected.diagram_topology_layout_fingerprint: FortiSwitch management SVI with passive ARP listener and active GARP probe branches converging on conflict log/SNMP trap.

selected.lesson_subject: WPA3 Beacon Protection: beacon MIC generation, VAP/profile assignment, and packet-level verification
selected.scenario_status: No directly matched recent FortiAP Community scenario was verified within the strict 30-day window.
selected.feature_mechanism_fingerprint: WPA3 Beacon Protection adds a Management MIC element to beacon frames and advertises the Beacon Protection capability; configuration is a VAP property, requires supported Wi-Fi 6E/Wi-Fi 7 AP hardware and FAP 7.6.1+, then must be assigned through the AP WTP profile.
selected.workflow_transaction_fingerprint: WPA3 VAP with PMF -> beacon-protection enabled -> VAP attached to WTP radio profile -> AP instantiates BSSID -> transmitted beacon includes Management MIC and Extended Capabilities beacon-protection flag.
selected.failure_class: Feature configured on an unsupported AP/firmware, not assigned to the active radio profile, or assumed enabled because WPA3/PMF alone is enabled.
selected.evidence_pattern: VAP CLI config; WTP profile radio VAP list; FortiAP `vcfg` output `beacon_prot=enabled`; wireless capture showing Management MIC element (tag 76), KeyID/IPN/MIC and Extended Capabilities flag.
selected.remediation_path: Confirm model and FAP release support; enable PMF and Beacon Protection on the WPA3 VAP; assign the VAP to the intended WTP profile/radio; verify AP runtime config and beacon capture from the air.
selected.question_fingerprint: Distinguish PMF from beacon integrity; identify the runtime output proving VAP assignment; interpret Management MIC in capture; identify unsupported model/firmware boundary.
selected.diagram_topology_layout_fingerprint: FortiGate wireless controller -> WPA3 VAP/PMF/Beacon Protection -> WTP profile/radio -> FortiAP beacon transmitter -> over-the-air MIC/capability capture.

selected.lesson_subject: Access Point Management: DHCP/DNS-based host state enforcement behind non-VLAN-aware APs and hubs
selected.scenario_status: Historical Community technical tip published 2023-04-25; used only as a scenario illustration, not presented as recent.
selected.feature_mechanism_fingerprint: When VLAN switching per endpoint is unavailable behind a bridging AP/hub, FortiNAC enforces host state through separate authorized/unauthorized DHCP pools and DNS behavior on a shared VLAN; DHCP lease membership is the authorization signal and unknown/static-IP hosts raise StaticIPAddress events.
selected.workflow_transaction_fingerprint: Host behind AP sends DHCP -> FortiNAC checks MAC in normal-host list/lease configuration -> authorized host receives production pool and production DNS; unauthorized host receives restricted pool and FortiNAC wildcard DNS -> Application Server redirects to state-specific portal; static address absent from lease triggers event/alarm mapping.
selected.failure_class: Unauthorized host obtains production DNS, authorized host receives isolation DNS, static IP bypasses DHCP state, or host remains on production network after a failed rescan until lease expiry/disconnect.
selected.evidence_pattern: AP port membership in Access-Point-Management group; AP removed from Bridging Devices group; DHCP relay points to FortiNAC; DHCP lease file; DNS answer; StaticIPAddress event and alarm action.
selected.remediation_path: Verify Configuration Wizard VLAN/IP pools; assign correct AP uplink port; remove bridging classification and user-defined uplink; point relay to FortiNAC; map StaticIPAddress event; account for lease expiry and feature removal in FortiNAC-F 7.6.
selected.question_fingerprint: Infer host state from DHCP pool and DNS; identify why VLAN switching is not required; interpret missing lease as static-IP event; identify rescan limitation.
selected.diagram_topology_layout_fingerprint: Shared VLAN with non-managed AP/hub -> DHCP relay to FortiNAC -> authorized and unauthorized pools/DNS branches -> production or captive/isolation portal.

selected.lesson_subject: Machine authentication with Active Directory compute-group RBAC: distinct host/user group mapping and EAP credential paths
selected.scenario_status: No directly matched recent FortiNAC-F Community scenario was verified in the strict 30-day window.
selected.feature_mechanism_fingerprint: FortiNAC-F 7.6 machine authentication uses AD computer credentials or EAP-TLS certificates; directory sync creates a `<group>_host` group mapping so a host identity can be assigned to a synchronized LDAP compute group; primary AD groups such as Domain Computers are not supported for this mapping.
selected.workflow_transaction_fingerprint: Domain-joined endpoint initiates machine 802.1X -> RADIUS Local Server validates MSCHAPv2 computer account or EAP-TLS certificate -> FortiNAC-F retrieves AD attributes/group membership -> host group is renamed `<group>_host` and selected as group attribute -> host record receives compute-group RBAC membership -> network access/compliance policy evaluates machine identity.
selected.failure_class: Computer account not domain joined, primary group not importable, certificate identity/hostname mismatch, or RADIUS TLS trust failure.
selected.evidence_pattern: Directory synchronization task; Groups view showing `<group>_host`; FortiNAC-F Inventory host identity; RADIUS session/EAP result; certificate CN/SAN/UPN and trusted root; Winbind domain status.
selected.remediation_path: Join endpoint to AD; use an ordinary LDAP security group instead of primary Domain Computers; synchronize directory; configure local RADIUS EAP type and certificate trust; on 7.6.3+ use Client Certificate Attribute only when hostname must be extracted from CN/DNS/UPN.
selected.question_fingerprint: Explain why primary Domain Computers is not mapped; identify host-group suffix; choose EAP-TLS certificate evidence; diagnose a valid user login that does not prove machine authorization.
selected.diagram_topology_layout_fingerprint: Domain-joined endpoint -> switch/AP 802.1X -> FortiNAC local RADIUS/EAP -> AD computer account and group sync -> separate host/user RBAC branches.

selected.lesson_subject: FIDO authentication for IdP-initiated SAML: username-only start, factor enforcement, and SP assertion delivery
selected.scenario_status: No directly matched recent FortiAuthenticator Community scenario was verified within the strict 30-day window.
selected.feature_mechanism_fingerprint: FortiAuthenticator SAML IdP can require FIDO authentication for IdP-initiated logins; user begins on a username-only Login Fido Page, completes configured FIDO/password validation, selects an authorized SP from the IdP portal, and FAC sends the SAML assertion response.
selected.workflow_transaction_fingerprint: Browser -> FAC IdP login portal -> username-only identification -> configured FIDO/password factors -> SP list filtered by user authorization -> user selects SP -> FAC creates signed assertion -> browser posts assertion to SP -> SP validates and authorizes.
selected.failure_class: IdP-initiated login unexpectedly offers wrong factor, user is not authorized for SP, FIDO registration/credential fails, or SP rejects assertion despite successful IdP authentication.
selected.evidence_pattern: SAML IdP General > IdP Initiated Login settings; replacement message page; user FIDO registration; SP authorization/group filter; SAML IdP event logs and SP assertion validation result.
selected.remediation_path: Set required IdP-initiated authentication method; ensure users are enrolled for FIDO and permitted fallback factors; verify SP user-source/group authorization; validate SP certificate, ACS/recipient and assertion acceptance separately.
selected.question_fingerprint: Distinguish IdP authentication from SP authorization; explain username-only FIDO start; infer why SP can reject after successful FIDO; identify the assertion delivery sequence.
selected.diagram_topology_layout_fingerprint: Browser -> FAC IdP portal -> FIDO/password factor gate -> authorized SP selector -> SAML assertion POST -> SP validation/resource.

selected.lesson_subject: Kerberos authentication for native RDP NLA: secret-derived realm, KDC discovery, and launcher boundary
selected.scenario_status: No directly matched recent FortiPAM Community troubleshooting scenario was verified within the strict 30-day window.
selected.feature_mechanism_fingerprint: FortiPAM native RDP launcher can use Kerberos instead of default NTLM for NLA/CredSSP; realm derives from domain configured on secret/target; KDC can be discovered through DNS SRV or overridden by explicit FQDN/IP and optional port (default 88).
selected.workflow_transaction_fingerprint: Secret enables RDP service + NLA + Use Kerberos -> target domain determines realm -> FortiPAM locates KDC via SRV or configured address -> requests Kerberos ticket using secret credentials -> native RDP NLA/CredSSP authenticates target.
selected.failure_class: Kerberos realm/KDC discovery mismatch, DNS/SPN/time/credential issue, wrong target FQDN, or feature expected to work in Web RDP/TCP-forwarding mode.
selected.evidence_pattern: Secret RDP Service settings; target Advanced Domain Settings KDC Address; DNS SRV resolution; KDC TCP/UDP 88 reachability; native launcher result; Windows Security log and Kerberos ticket state.
selected.remediation_path: Use target FQDN and Windows Domain Account secret; set NLA and Use Kerberos for NLA; confirm domain/realm, DNS SRV and time synchronization; specify KDC Address only when auto-discovery is unsuitable; use native RDP launcher.
selected.question_fingerprint: Identify why IP-only target breaks realm/SPN assumptions; distinguish native launcher from Web RDP; determine when explicit KDC is needed; explain NLA versus standard RDP TLS.
selected.diagram_topology_layout_fingerprint: FortiPAM secret/target -> realm derivation -> DNS SRV or explicit KDC:88 -> Kerberos ticket -> native RDP NLA/CredSSP -> Windows target.

selected.lesson_subject: FortiSIEM 7.5 Federated Search: provider credentials, external datastores, observable-column mappings, and ClickHouse result reuse
selected.scenario_status: No directly matched recent FortiSIEM Community scenario was verified within the strict 30-day window.
selected.feature_mechanism_fingerprint: FortiSIEM 7.5 Federated Search is available for ClickHouse deployments and queries external data stores (AWS Security Lake, AWS S3, FortiEDR, PostgreSQL, MySQL, Snowflake); requires provider credentials, datastore/table definitions, and mappings from FortiSIEM observables to external columns; search results are persisted in ClickHouse for Advanced Search and can be pivoted from Incidents/Analytics.
selected.workflow_transaction_fingerprint: Define provider credentials -> add provider datastore/table -> map FortiSIEM observable to external column -> launch Federated Search or pivot from Incident/Analytics -> connector queries external data -> result set stored in ClickHouse -> Advanced Search, PDF/email or Case attachment.
selected.failure_class: Provider authentication/scope failure, missing or incorrect observable mapping, unsupported deployment type, or external datastore schema drift.
selected.evidence_pattern: Deployment type (ClickHouse); provider connectivity/credentials; datastore/table definition; attribute mapping; query result set; ClickHouse stored result visible to Advanced Search; export/case attachment.
selected.remediation_path: Confirm ClickHouse deployment; validate provider access and least-privilege credentials; verify table/schema and column mapping for each observable; test a known indicator; compare external source result to persisted ClickHouse result; revise mapping after schema changes.
selected.question_fingerprint: Identify why Federated Search is unavailable on non-ClickHouse; order provider/datastore/mapping prerequisites; distinguish a source-query miss from an attribute-mapping miss; explain why result is available to Advanced Search after execution.
selected.diagram_topology_layout_fingerprint: FortiSIEM Incident/Analytics -> Federated Search -> provider credentials -> external datastore/table -> observable-column mapping -> ClickHouse result store -> Advanced Search/PDF/Case.

selected.lesson_subject: HTTP/3 QUIC inspection: security-profile action, traffic-scope boundary, and proxy-user fallback
selected.scenario_status: No directly matched recent FortiSASE Community scenario was verified; older FortiGate QUIC articles were not promoted to FortiSASE scenario evidence.
selected.feature_mechanism_fingerprint: FortiSASE adds an HTTP/3 QUIC inspection action within security profile groups; Inspect allows HTTP/3 and exposes it to applicable security features, Bypass allows without inspection, Block rejects QUIC so clients generally fall back to HTTP/2; setting applies to agent and edge-device traffic but not proxy-policy traffic.
selected.workflow_transaction_fingerprint: Agent/edge endpoint sends UDP/443 QUIC -> security profile group SSL inspection action evaluates Inspect/Bypass/Block -> Inspect permits security engines to process HTTP/3; Block forces client fallback to HTTP/2 in most cases; proxy-user path requires endpoint/browser QUIC disablement if deep inspection is required.
selected.failure_class: Security profile action mismatch, proxy traffic incorrectly assumed to inherit agent/edge QUIC inspection, or browser silently falls back to HTTP/2 after QUIC block.
selected.evidence_pattern: Feature-version entitlement; security profile group SSL inspection action; endpoint/edge versus proxy-user traffic classification; browser DevTools protocol column (`h3` versus `h2`); UDP/443 session logs.
selected.remediation_path: Confirm Feature-version capability and traffic type; set Inspect/Bypass/Block deliberately in security profile group; for proxy users disable browser QUIC where inspection is required; verify protocol negotiation and logs instead of assuming UDP/443 proves HTTP/3 inspection.
selected.question_fingerprint: Distinguish agent/edge traffic from proxy policy; infer effect of Block versus Bypass; interpret h3/h2 browser evidence; identify why profile action is unavailable without certificate/deep inspection.
selected.diagram_topology_layout_fingerprint: Agent/edge QUIC UDP/443 path through security profile action with Inspect/Bypass/Block branches; separate proxy-user path with browser QUIC disable/fallback.

selected.lesson_subject: Dual-server Performance SLA target selection: sequential probe-target fallback and link-failure confirmation
selected.scenario_status: Historical Community discussion dated 2026-03-13; used only to contrast one SLA with two probe targets versus two independent SLAs. Official guide controls the exact sequential target-selection mechanics.
selected.feature_mechanism_fingerprint: A single SD-WAN Performance SLA can configure up to two servers; FortiGate probes the first, switches to the second if the first is unavailable, remains on the second until it fails, then returns to the first; SLA fails only when both servers are unavailable. This protects against false link-down caused by one target outage.
selected.workflow_transaction_fingerprint: Health-check participant sends protocol-specific probe to primary target -> target availability determines active probe destination -> if primary unavailable, probe target switches to secondary -> if both unavailable, member health-check fails -> route/member eligibility is withdrawn subject to fail/recovery thresholds.
selected.failure_class: False-positive link-down from a single probe target outage; false confidence from a probe target that does not represent the service path; confusing one health-check with multiple independent SLAs.
selected.evidence_pattern: `diagnose sys sdwan health-check`; Performance SLA server list and current server; member state/packet loss/latency/jitter; route removal/recovery; probe packet capture.
selected.remediation_path: Choose two independent and representative targets reachable over every participant; configure protocol and check interval/fail/recovery thresholds; test loss of each target separately; distinguish server fallback from link-quality SLA thresholds and from multiple independent health checks.
selected.question_fingerprint: Predict behavior when first target alone fails; explain why second target avoids false link-down; distinguish sequential dual-server fallback from two separate SLAs; interpret health-check fail only after both targets fail.
selected.diagram_topology_layout_fingerprint: SD-WAN member -> primary probe server with fallback to secondary probe server -> health-check state machine -> SLA/member route eligibility.
